newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government plays down mini-budget upset.
newsitem.headline: Italy government plays down mini-budget upset.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government insisted on Friday that a lower house commission's rejection of a proposed 1997 mini-budget would have no major political repercussions and problems would be overcome.
The house's budget commission voted 25 to 24 against the mini-budget, which will now go to the full Chamber of Deputies for a vote on the package.

Opponents seized on the vote as a considerable embarrassment that underlined the government's fragility after a year in office and again showed up the tensions among the various elements of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition.
"Today's evidence shows that this government is made up of zombies, walking dead," said far-right National Alliance deputy Maurizio Gasparri.
National Alliance party leader Gianfranco Fini called the defeat politically serious and warned: "Prodi should not minimise what has happened."

Mauro Paissan, a senior member of the Greens party which is part of Prodi's coalition, said the commission had effectively challenged the government to put the mini-budget to a confidence test in the full chamber.
"Basically, what the (government) majority and the opposition have done is to ask the government to call a confidence vote," he told reporters.
Prodi, speaking in the north-eastern town of Gorizia, said he was "calm" about the defeat at commission stage while his deputy Walter Veltroni also played it down.
"It does not create political problems and does not call into question the solidarity of the majority," he said.
"We will find a solution in the Chamber, we shall see what it will be," Veltroni added.

Industry Minister Pierluigi Bersani told reporters in Naples that he thought a confidence vote would be needed. "I think the government, with its majority, will find the parliamentary tools needed to pass the mini-budget," he added.

Communist refoundation, a regular thorn in the government's side in the past, voted for the mini-budget and the two dissenters in Friday's vote said they would also fall back in line if it came to a confidence test.
The two were former members of Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini's Italian Renewal group in parliament. Dini's party voted with the government for the mini-budget.
"If the government should call a confidence vote, we will vote with them because we don't want a crisis," said Giuseppe Bicocchi of the tiny Segni Pact group, one of the rebels.

The supplementary budget aims to reduce the 1997 budget deficit by 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) in the hope of keeping Italy on track to meet the deficit target needed to join Europe's planned single currency.
Some measures in the package have been severely criticised by the opposition Freedom Alliance and industry.

Italian financial markets were already recording losses before the vote on concerns that Italy is set to miss the deficit target but they dipped further on the news before recovering to pre-vote levels.

The lira was quoted close to the day's lows at 988 per mark by 1345 GMT, the key government bond futures contract on LIFFE fell half a point before recovering and the blue-chip Mib30 share index finished 0.85 percent down at 18,220.
